questions.stem: Dr. Jones has moved to San Francisco for her fellowship and has performed a study looking at risk factors for the development of infection with Cryptococcus. She created a retrospective cohort of all patients admitted to her institution and compared those with cryptococcosis and those without. While analyzing the demographics, she calculated that male patients have 2.1-fold (95% CI 1.7, 2.4) higher odds of developing cryptococcosis than women. Very excitedly, she shows the data to her advisor, who points out that HIV is more prevalent in men who have sex with men, and that HIV also predisposes for cryptococcosis. When adjusting for the diagnosis of HIV , Dr. Jones found no effect.
questions.lead_in: In this situation, HIV is behaving as a(n):
questions.explanation: Confounder Confounder is the correct answer, because in this example cryptococcal infection was associated with HIV infection, and HIV is more prevalent in men who have sex with men. While it initially appeared that the infection was associated with male sex, the relationship was distorted by the third variable (confounder), which is HIV infection. The dependent variable (outcome) in this example is cryptococcosis. HIV infection is a yes/no variable and thus not an ordinal variable (categorical variable with order) nor is it a continuous variable (quantitative).

questions.question: Explain the post-antibiotic effect (PAE).

parts.text: Explain the post-antibiotic effect (PAE).

parts_raw.text: Explain PAE.

questions.model_answer: a) PAE is the persistent suppression of bacterial growth after brief exposure to an antimicrobial, continuing after drug concentrations have fallen below the MIC (and after the drug is cleared from the site). It reflects sublethal damage/slow recovery of the organism rather than residual drug activity, and it permits dosing intervals during which concentrations are below the MIC (e.g., once-daily aminoglycosides). Prolonged PAE against gram-negatives is seen with aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones; beta-lactams show little or no PAE against gram-negative bacilli (but do against staphylococci/streptococci).

cohort_answer.text: Continued killing/ persistent bacterial suppression after the antimicrobial is metabolized or cleared.

questions.question: An infant has infant botulism. Give the specific therapy.

parts.text: Give the specific therapy.

parts_raw.text: Specific therapy

questions.model_answer: a) Human-derived botulism immune globulin intravenous (BIG-IV, BabyBIG) given as early as possible, plus meticulous supportive/respiratory care; avoid aminoglycosides (and other neuromuscular blocking agents), which can potentiate the neuromuscular blockade. questions.question: A child develops hemolytic uremic syndrome after Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli infection. Give three laboratory findings.

parts.text: Give three laboratory findings.

parts_raw.text: 3 laboratory findings

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — anemia with schistocytes on smear, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, negative direct Coombs test. (2) Thrombocytopenia (typically <150 x 10^9/L) with normal INR/PTT and fibrinogen. (3) Acute kidney injury — rising creatinine with hematuria/proteinuria.

cohort_answer.text: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, AKI, coombs' negative, schistocytes

questions.question: Describe primary, secondary and tertiary prevention and give an example of each.

parts.text: Describe primary, secondary and tertiary prevention and give an example of each.

parts_raw.text: Describe Primary, secondary and tertiary prevention and example of each

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Primary prevention — preventing disease before it occurs by removing exposure or increasing host resistance; example: immunization (e.g., hepatitis B vaccine), condom use, pre-exposure prophylaxis. (2) Secondary prevention — detecting disease in an asymptomatic/early stage so treatment can prevent progression and transmission; example: screening for latent tuberculosis infection, HIV or syphilis screening, cervical cancer screening. (3) Tertiary prevention — limiting disability and complications once disease is established; example: antiretroviral therapy with opportunistic-infection prophylaxis in advanced HIV, or diabetic foot care to prevent osteomyelitis.

cohort_answer.text: Primary: intervening before health effects occur (vaccinations, altering risky behaviors, banning substances). Secondary: screening to identify diseases in earliest stages before symptoms (mammography, blood pressure testing, ASA for CAD). Tertiary: managing disease post-diagnosis to slow/stop progression (chemotherapy, cardiac/stroke rehab, screening for complications).

questions.question: Post-antibiotic effect.

parts.text: Define it.
What class has this?

parts_raw.text: Define
What class has this?

questions.model_answer:
a) Persistent suppression of bacterial growth after brief antimicrobial exposure, continuing after the drug concentration has fallen below the organism's MIC.
b) Aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones (prolonged PAE, including against gram-negative bacilli); other protein-synthesis inhibitors (macrolides, clindamycin, tetracyclines, linezolid) also show PAE. cohort_answer.text: Definition: The ability of an antibiotic to continue having sustained effect/bacterial killing even after concentration drops below the measured MIC. Classes: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones; most other inhibitors of protein synthesis (Clindamycin, macrolides, tetracyclines).

Give two examples for each.

parts_raw.text: a) Name two ways that antimicrobials display unique pharmacodynamics
b) Give two examples for each.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Concentration-dependent killing — efficacy driven by peak/MIC (Cmax/MIC) or 24-h AUC/MIC. (2) Time-dependent killing — efficacy driven by the percentage of the dosing interval that free drug concentration exceeds the MIC (T>MIC).
b) Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones (also daptomycin). Time-dependent: penicillins, cephalosporins (also carbapenems); AUC/MIC-driven agents include vancomycin and tetracyclines.

cohort_answer.text: a) Time/MIC; Concentration/MIC; AUC/MIC. b) Time/MIC: Beta lactams, cephalosporins, Clindamycin. Concentration/MIC: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Macrolides. AUC/MIC: Vancomycin, Tetracyclines.

questions.question: There is a study of a test for a new pathogen called Examination panicuum, which included 100 patients with the disease (of which 95 tested positive for the disease), and 50 patients without the disease (of which 5 patients tested positive).
questions.question_raw: There is a study of a test for a new pathogen called Examination panicuum, which included 100 patients with the disease (of which 95 tested positive for the disease), and 50 patients without the disease (of which 5 patients tested positive).

parts.text: What is the sensitivity of this test?
What is the specificity of this test?
What is the positive predictive value of this test?
Which of the measures listed above will be affected by the low prevalence rate of this disease in your area?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the sensitivity of this test?
b) What is the specificity of this test?
c) What is the positive predictive value of this test?
d) Which of the measures listed above will be affected by the low prevalence rate of this disease in your area?

questions.model_answer:
a) Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 95/100 = 95%.
b) Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = (50-5)/50 = 45/50 = 90%.
c) PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 95/(95+5) = 95/100 = 95% (in this study population, prevalence 100/150).
d) The positive predictive value. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence; PPV falls as prevalence falls (and NPV rises), so in a low-prevalence area the same test yields far more false-positive than true-positive results.

cohort_answer.text: Sensitivity: 95/100 = 95%. Specificity: 45/50 = 90%. PPV: 95/100 = 95%. PPV is affected by low prevalence of disease - as prevalence increases, PPV increases, as prevalence decreases, PPV decreases.

questions.question: You are asked to choose between two antimicrobials, Drug A and Drug B, for this patient.
questions.question_raw: Repeat question: I'd choose Drug A over Drug B, because…

parts.text: Explain your choice.

parts_raw.text: Explain your choice.

questions.model_answer: a) Justify the choice on the standard axes, applied to the specific case: (1) spectrum and reliable in vitro activity against the identified or most likely pathogen, with the narrowest adequate spectrum; (2) pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics — penetration to the site of infection (CSF, bone, lung, urine, abscess, vegetation), bactericidal versus bacteriostatic activity where required (endocarditis, meningitis, neutropenia), and achievable target attainment; (3) evidence of clinical efficacy for the syndrome; (4) safety — toxicity, allergy, organ dysfunction and drug interactions in this patient; (5) practicality and stewardship — oral bioavailability/route, dosing frequency, monitoring requirements, resistance-selection pressure and cost.

questions.question: Given a 2x2 table of test results against disease status, calculate test performance characteristics.

parts.text: Calculate sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value. Which parameters change with disease prevalence?

parts_raw.text: Calculate Sensitivity, Specificity, Positive Predictive Value. Which parameters change with disease prevalence?

questions.model_answer:
Using a 2x2 table with TP (test+/disease+), FP (test+/disease-), FN (test-/disease+), TN (test-/disease-):
Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) - proportion of diseased correctly identified.
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) - proportion of non-diseased correctly identified.
Positive predictive value = TP / (TP + FP) - probability disease is present given a positive test.
Worked example (TP 90, FN 10, FP 100, TN 800): Sn = 90/100 = 90%; Sp = 800/900 = 89%; PPV = 90/190 = 47%.
Prevalence dependence: sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test and do NOT change with prevalence; PPV and NPV DO change - PPV rises and NPV falls as prevalence rises, so the same test performs poorly (low PPV, many false positives) in a low-prevalence population. Likelihood ratios (LR+ = Sn/(1-Sp), LR- = (1-Sn)/Sp) are also prevalence-independent.

If the intended organism is cytomegalovirus (the usual framing of this question), four presentations in an immunocompetent host are: (1) asymptomatic infection (the majority); (2) heterophile-negative infectious mononucleosis - prolonged fever, fatigue, atypical lymphocytosis, mild transaminitis, splenomegaly; (3) organ-specific disease such as hepatitis, colitis (often in older adults or with inflammatory bowel disease), pneumonitis, or myocarditis; (4) neurologic/other complications - Guillain-Barre syndrome, meningoencephalitis, retinitis, or thrombosis (venous thromboembolism associated with acute CMV). questions.question: Basic reproduction number (R0).

parts.text: Define R0.
Rank the following R0 values from highest to lowest: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, 2009 pandemic H1N1 influenza, measles, varicella-zoster virus.
What does R0 need to be in order to have a growing epidemic?

parts_raw.text: Define R0
Rank following R0 from highest to lowest: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, 2009 pandemic H1N1 flu, measles, VZV
What does R0 need to be in order to have a growing epidemic

questions.model_answer:
a) R0 is the basic reproduction number: the average number of secondary cases generated by one infectious case introduced into a wholly susceptible population, in the absence of immunity or intervention. It is a product of transmission probability per contact, contact rate, and duration of infectiousness. (Re/Rt is the effective reproduction number in a partly immune or intervened population.)
b) Measles (12-18) > varicella-zoster virus (10-12) > SARS-CoV (2-4) > 2009 pandemic H1N1 influenza (~1.5-1.6) > MERS-CoV (<1, ~0.5-0.9).
c) R0 (or Re) must be greater than 1 for the epidemic to grow; = 1 means endemic/stable transmission; < 1 means the outbreak dies out. Herd immunity threshold = 1 - 1/R0.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell epidemiology of infectious diseases chapter; R0 estimates per WHO/CDC outbreak literature.

cohort_answer.text: Definition: Number of people that one person can spread infection to on average. Ranking: Measles 12-18 > VZV 10-12 > SARS-CoV 2-4 (wildtype, omicron higher 9-21) > H1N1 flu 1.6 > MERS-CoV 0.5. Growing epidemic: R0 needs to be >1. (Mpox ~2)

questions.question: Define the following epidemiologic terms.

parts.text: Define: Endemic
Define: Epidemic
Define: Pandemic

parts_raw.text: Define: Endemic
Define: Epidemic
Define: Pandemic

questions.model_answer:
a) Endemic: the constant, expected presence of a disease at a baseline level within a defined geographic area or population group (e.g. malaria in sub-Saharan Africa); incidence is persistent and predictable.
b) Epidemic (or outbreak, when localized): occurrence of cases of a disease clearly in excess of the expected baseline for that population, place, and time period, usually with person-to-person or common-source spread.
c) Pandemic: an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents, affecting a large number of people (e.g. 2009 H1N1, SARS-CoV-2).

cohort_answer.text: Endemic: Disease that is prevalent in or restricted to a particular location, region, or population. Epidemic: Disease affecting many people at the same time, and spreading from person to person in a locality where the disease is not permanently prevalent. Pandemic: An epidemic disease that has spread over a large area affecting a substantial number of individuals

questions.question: Differentiate Th1 and Th2 responses.

parts.text: Differentiate Th1 and Th2 responses.

parts_raw.text: Differentiate Th1 and Th2 responses

questions.model_answer:
Th1: induced by IL-12 and IFN-gamma (signalling via STAT1/STAT4, transcription factor T-bet). Signature cytokines IFN-gamma, IL-2, TNF/lymphotoxin. Function: classical (M1) macrophage activation, enhanced killing of intracellular pathogens, opsonizing/complement-fixing IgG, delayed-type hypersensitivity. Protective against intracellular organisms - Mycobacterium tuberculosis, non-typhoidal Salmonella, Leishmania, Listeria; defects in the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis cause Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease. Clinical correlate: tuberculoid leprosy, granuloma formation.
Th2: induced by IL-4 (STAT6, transcription factor GATA3). Signature cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (also IL-9, IL-10, amphiregulin). Function: IgE class switching, eosinophil recruitment and activation, mast cell activation, mucus hypersecretion and smooth muscle contraction, alternative (M2) macrophage activation. Protective against helminths; drives atopy and asthma. Clinical correlate: lepromatous leprosy (high antibody, poor cell-mediated control, high bacillary load). The two subsets are mutually cross-inhibitory (IFN-gamma suppresses Th2; IL-4/IL-10 suppress Th1).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell innate/adaptive immunity chapters (Abbas cellular immunology framework).

cohort_answer.text: Th1: driven by IFN-gamma and IL-12; secretes IFN-gamma, activates macrophages/DCs, enhances killing of intracellular microbes and APC function; also secretes IL2, TNF, lymphotoxin; key role against intracellular organisms (Salmonella, MTB, Leishmania); STAT1/4 pathway; associated with tuberculoid leprosy. Th2: driven by IL-4; signature cytokines IL-4/5/13 (also 9/10/25/amphiregulin); GATA3 pathway; contributes to allergic/atopic disease; important against helminth infections of GI tract; assists eosinophil recruitment, IgE production, mucus hypersecretion; associated with lepromatous leprosy.

questions.question: Toll-like receptors.

parts.text: What do they recognize and what do they do?
Name one clinical drug that utilizes a Toll-like receptor and its clinical use.

parts_raw.text: What do they recognize and what do they do?
One clinical drug that utilizes TLR and its clinical use?

questions.model_answer:
a) Toll-like receptors are germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors of the innate immune system, expressed on monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils and epithelium - on the cell surface (TLR1, 2, 4, 5, 6) or in endosomes (TLR3, 7, 8, 9). They recognize conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns: LPS (TLR4), lipopeptides/peptidoglycan/lipoarabinomannan (TLR1/2/6), flagellin (TLR5), dsRNA (TLR3), ssRNA (TLR7/8), unmethylated CpG DNA (TLR9); they also sense host damage-associated molecular patterns. Ligation signals through MyD88 (or TRIF for TLR3/4) to NF-kappaB and IRF3/7, producing pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) and type I interferons, upregulating costimulatory molecules, and thereby linking innate recognition to adaptive immunity.
b) Imiquimod, a TLR7 agonist, applied topically for anogenital warts (HPV), and also used for superficial basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratosis. (Other acceptable answers: BCG intravesical therapy, or the TLR4 agonist MPL adjuvant AS04/AS01 in HPV and recombinant zoster vaccines; CpG-1018 adjuvant in HepB-CpG vaccine is a TLR9 agonist.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell innate immunity chapter; vaccine adjuvant examples per product monographs.

cohort_answer.text: A) TLRs are pattern recognizing protein structures of innate immune system, expressed on leukocyte populations; recognize preserved microbial antigens (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, nucleic acid parts). B) Imiquimod - TLR-7 agonist; useful in slowing malignancy growth and inhibiting viral replication (e.g. HPV); topical administration associated with increased cytokine/immune cell markers.

questions.question: Describe Toll-like receptors: what they are and what their function is. Name two microbes recognized by Toll-like receptors.
questions.question_raw: Describe TLR: what are they, what is their function. Name 2 microbes recognized by TLR

parts.text: Name two microbes recognized by Toll-like receptors.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 microbes recognized by TLR

questions.model_answer: (1) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - lipoarabinomannan/lipoproteins sensed by TLR2 (with TLR1); TLR1 polymorphisms are associated with leprosy susceptibility. (2) Plasmodium falciparum - GPI anchors and haemozoin sensed by TLR4/TLR9. (Other acceptable pairs: Neisseria meningitidis and Borrelia burgdorferi via TLR2/TLR4; influenza or HIV ssRNA via TLR7/8; herpes simplex virus dsDNA via TLR9, with TLR3 deficiency causing HSV encephalitis; Legionella flagellin via TLR5.)

cohort_answer.text: Mycobacteria, Malaria. (TLR1/2 - Mycobacteria, Gram positive bacteria, Neisseria spp, B. burgdorferi; TLR2/6 - dsDNA viruses; TLR4 - RSV, Chlamydia, malaria; TLR7 - ssRNA viruses (HIV, influenza); TLR8 - ssRNA viruses; TLR3 mutation associated with HSV encephalitis, TLR4 with meningococcemia, TLR1 with leprosy, TLR5 with legionella.)
